summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing the IS-IS routing protocol when it is used to build routing tables for IP networks. It lets network management tools inspect and configure IS-IS routers. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Routers talk to each other to find the best roads. This gives the people running them a control panel to look at and adjust how one such conversation goes.

questions: how to monitor is-is adjacencies with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP MIB module that lets management tools inspect and configure IS-IS routers carrying IP traffic.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to look at and configure IS-IS, a link-state routing protocol, on routers from different vendors that use it to build IP routing tables.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ISIS-MIB module, registered as { mib-2 138 }, with tables for system settings, circuits, adjacencies, reachable addresses and the link state database, plus counters and notifications.
tldr.outcome: Management stations can read and set IS-IS state with SNMP. Because writable objects can disrupt routing, the RFC recommends SNMPv3 security whenever write access is offered.

today: RFC 4444 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the ISIS-MIB module published in this document.

sections.title: Scope and Management Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the IS-IS routing protocol, as described in ISO 10589, when it is used to build routing tables for IP networks as described in RFC 1195. MIB objects are generally accessed with the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and they are defined using the Structure of Management Information, here SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).

The objects are mainly derived from the definitions in ISO 10589 and ISO 10733, with extra objects for the IP-specific parts of Integrated IS-IS. The module is based on a 1994 IETF document by Chris Gunner, updated to current syntax, with portions that are not relevant to IP left out and management support for current practice added.
sections.eli5: IS-IS is a way for routers to share road maps. This RFC lists everything about it that a person can look at or change from a management program.

sections.title: What the MIB Contains
sections.content:
The module is organised into groups of tables:

  • System-wide attributes: isisSystem for one IS-IS instance on a router, manually configured and learned area addresses, summary addresses, route redistribution criteria and a router table holding host names and router IDs.
  • Level attributes: isisSysLevel, for a domain (Level 2) or an area (Level 1).
  • Circuit attributes: isisCirc and isisCircLevel for point-to-point or broadcast interfaces.
  • Counters for the system, for circuits and for packets by type.
  • Adjacency attributes for neighbouring routers, reachable address tables, the link state PDU tables and the objects carried in notifications.

The module also manages Mesh Groups (RFC 2973) and the three-way handshake for point-to-point adjacencies (RFC 3373). It imports definitions from several other MIBs, including the Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863) and the Internet address types (RFC 4001).
sections.eli5: The control panel is split into sections, like a car dashboard: one for the whole router, one for each cable plugged in, one for the neighbours, and one for warning lights and counters.

sections.title: Textual Conventions and Layout
sections.content:
The module first defines textual conventions, reusable value types. Examples include a 6-byte system ID, an 8-byte Link State PDU ID made of the 6-byte system ID, a one-byte pseudonode ID (0 unless the LSP describes a LAN) and a one-byte fragment number, and an LSP buffer size between 512 and 16000.

Metrics come in several widths. The default metric is a 6-bit value from 0 to 63 and, in the RFC's words, only the default metric is used in practice. Wide metrics for IS neighbours are 24 bits and full metrics for IP routes are 32 bits, following the Traffic Engineering extensions in RFC 3784. A metric style object selects narrow, wide or both (RFC 3787).

Three behaviours are described for objects: ResettingTimer for interval objects that change while the protocol runs, ReplaceOnlyWhileDisabled for objects that cannot change while the row is administratively on, and ManualOrAutomatic for objects that are read-write only when created manually. Configured values MUST survive an agent reboot.
sections.eli5: Before the dials are described, the RFC defines the kinds of numbers they use, such as how big an ID can be and how long a path cost can get, so everyone reads the dials the same way.

sections.title: System and Circuit Settings
sections.content:
The system objects hold the settings of one IS-IS instance. Examples are the levels it runs at (isisSysLevelType, default level 1 and 2), the system ID, the maximum number of equal-cost paths to split between (1 to 32, default 2), the maximum interval between generated LSPs (default 900 seconds), the wait time before moving from waiting to on (default 60 seconds) and the lifetime placed in generated LSPs (isisSysMaxAge, default 1200 seconds). The administrative state defaults to off.

At most 3 manually configured area addresses can be active in one instance, and at least one must be active. Per level, an administrator can set the overload condition, and the level state shows as off, on, waiting or overloaded.

Circuits are the interfaces. A circuit has a type (broadcast, point-to-point and others), an administrative state, optional passive mode, mesh group membership and the three-way handshake switch. The circuit-level table holds per-level metrics, the IS priority, hello and CSNP timers, and LSP throttling and retransmission intervals.
sections.eli5: The router has a few big switches, like on or off and which levels to join, and each cable has its own small knobs, like how often to say hello to the neighbour.

sections.title: Adjacencies, Addresses and the LSP Database
sections.content:
The adjacency table describes neighbouring routers. Entries cannot be created by management action: they are established through the Hello protocol. An adjacency state is down, initializing, up or failed, and further tables list the area addresses, IP addresses and supported protocols that neighbours reported in their hello PDUs.

Two tables describe addresses a router knows by configuration or learned from another protocol: one for OSI reachable addresses and one for IP reachable addresses. Summary addresses let an administrator combine IP reachability announcements. If the router can reach any subset of the summary address, the summary MUST be announced instead, at the configured metric.

The LSP database is exposed in two tables. The summary table shows the header information of stored Link State PDUs, and the TLV table holds the sequence of TLVs that make up an LSP fragment.
sections.eli5: The neighbour list shows who the router is currently friends with and how healthy each friendship is. The map section shows which places it knows how to reach and the notes it has stored from others.

sections.title: Counters and Notifications
sections.content:
Counters record events at three levels. System counters track things such as corrupted LSPs, authentication type and authentication failures, sequence number skips, own LSP purges, partition changes and SPF runs. Circuit counters track adjacency changes, initialization failures, rejected adjacencies and ID field length mismatches. Packet counters break IS-IS PDUs down by type, such as hellos, LSPs, CSNPs and PSNPs, per level and direction.

The module also defines notifications for events such as database overload, corrupted LSPs, authentication failures, version skew, area mismatches, rejected adjacencies, oversized LSPs and adjacency changes. The adjacency change notification fires when an adjacency enters or leaves state up. All of them are controlled by one switch, isisSysNotificationEnable, which defaults to true.
sections.eli5: Counters are like a tally of how many times something odd happened. Notifications are the warning lights that flash when something important changes, such as a neighbour dropping off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This MIB may manage an IP router, so writable objects can be used for attacks. By raising or lowering metrics, traffic may be steered toward insecure parts of the network. Disabling the protocol on an interface can partition the network, and topology changes force every router to recompute its routes.

The RFC groups the writable objects by the harm they can cause, such as dropping an adjacency, splitting the network, causing intermittent outages, redirecting traffic, delaying convergence, avoiding detection by turning off notifications, preventing updates with mesh groups, and hijacking a LAN by changing the IS priority. It also lists a few objects that pose no known risk.

Read access does not add risk, because the values are readily visible to an intruder with access to traffic. If write access is provided, the RFC RECOMMENDED using the SNMPv3 security features, including cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can turn the dials can mess up the whole road system, so only trusted people should be allowed to change them, and the control panel should check who they are.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The only IANA action is the object identifier for the module. isisMIB is registered in the SMI Numbers registry as { mib-2 138 }. Beneath it, isisNotifications is 0, isisObjects is 1 and isisConformance is 2, and the ten object groups sit under isisObjects.
sections.eli5: Every dial needs a unique address in a big directory. The RFC claims one address for the whole IS-IS control panel and numbers the sections beneath it.

fields.desc: 0 unless the LSP represents the topology of a LAN.
